name: Camera angle / eye dominance selection
lead: Camera angle and eye dominance selection is the practice of choosing which side of the face, and which angle and distance, to present to a camera so that a person's features photograph at their best. People use it to look more symmetric, more balanced and better proportioned in photos, video calls and dating-profile pictures, sometimes with reference to a dominant eye.

Research on facial symmetry reports that faces are not perfectly symmetric: on average the eyes, nose and mouth sit slightly to the left relative to the ears, so the right side of the face appears larger [1]. Symmetry increases attractiveness ratings, more so for female faces [1]. This gives the practice its rationale: showing the side or angle that reads as more symmetric or better proportioned.

Distance and lens also change how a face is captured. Photography references note that close camera distances with wide-angle lenses make the nose look large relative to the rest of the face, while stepping back and using a moderate telephoto length produces a flatter, more even look [4]. A 2018 study in JAMA Facial Plastic Surgery modelled that a selfie from about 12 inches makes the base of the nose look roughly 30% wider and the tip about 7% wider than a portrait from five feet [5].

Ocular dominance is the tendency to prefer visual input from one eye; about 70% of people are right-eye dominant and 29% left-eye dominant, and it is mainly studied for aiming tasks [2]. Some people use it as a rule for choosing a side to show; no published study links eye dominance to a flattering camera side.

paras: The face is systematically offset: the eyes, nose and mouth are on average slightly left relative to the ears. This aurofacial asymmetry is about 2 degrees at birth and about 0.5 degrees in adults. During speech, 76% of people show greater mouth movement on the right side.[1]
Researchers caution that mirroring one half of a face to create a symmetric image can produce artificial features, such as an oversized or undersized nose.[1]

Eye dominance is only loosely analogous to handedness, and the dominant eye and dominant hand often differ. It can shift with gaze direction, task and fatigue. Tests include the Miles and Porta tests, the Dolman method and lens fogging.[2] The article notes that dominance matters for aiming sports and monovision contact lenses, and that fMRI shows brain activity differences in face perception by dominance, which concern how faces are processed and not how they look.[2]

Perspective distortion is the best-documented camera factor. Close distance with a wide-angle lens enlarges whatever is nearest the lens, typically the nose, and can distort expression; moderate telephoto focal lengths of roughly 85 to 135 mm on a 35 mm camera are described as flattering for portraits [4]. The JAMA Facial Plastic Surgery model compared a 12-inch selfie with a five-foot portrait and reported the nose-base and nose-tip widening above; the senior author described a selfie as a 'portable funhouse mirror' [5]. The authors noted that they did not test whether the distortion drives people to seek surgery [6].
A perception experiment found that recognition of unfamiliar faces in pictures was affected by perspective transformation tied to camera distance [6].
A 2013 study in the journal Laterality asked whether the advent of the camera changed the side of the face that artists chose to show in self-portraits.[3]

No studies found on choosing a camera side by eye dominance. Related research covers facial asymmetry and attractiveness [1], the orientation artists chose for self-portraits [3], face recognition under perspective changes [6] and modelled selfie-distance distortion [5].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, camera angle is discussed as a way to control how the face reads on video calls and in photos, including how phone distance and height change the look of the nose, eyes and jawline [7].

claims.claim: Holding the phone at certain heights and cutting off part of the face on screen can hide lens distortion and emphasise eyes and jawline.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org guide recommends framing so the midface is partly out of shot and the lower-angle view emphasises the jaw, and a reply says a lower phone position makes profile shots show more forward growth [7].
claims.experts: Photography references and the selfie-distance model report that short distances enlarge the nose and distort proportions [4][5]; no study has tested the specific framing tactics described.

claims.claim: A person's 'good side' can be chosen by facial asymmetry.
claims.believers: Posters say one side of the face looks better and that showing it improves photos.
claims.experts: Facial symmetry research reports small average left-right offsets and higher attractiveness ratings for symmetric faces; it does not state that a particular side is preferred [1].

claims.claim: The dominant eye determines the best camera side.
claims.believers: Some people choose the side matching their dominant eye.
claims.experts: Ocular dominance research concerns aiming and vision tasks [2]; no published study links it to a flattering camera side.

card.summary: Picking a 'better side' for photos; faces are measurably asymmetric, but no source links eye dominance to a flattering angle.
card.note: Research covers general facial asymmetry; eye dominance as a selection rule is untested.

quick.overview:
Many people photograph from a preferred side of the face, and some tie that choice to eye dominance.

Faces are known to be slightly asymmetric on average, but the sources reviewed do not say either side is preferred, and none links eye dominance to a flattering angle.
quick.mechanism: People pick the side or angle they judge as more symmetric or flattering. Eye dominance is the preference for one eye's visual input, about 70% right-dominant.
quick.risks: No physical risks. The practice is untested for effect on perceived attractiveness.

chain: Pick the side, angle and distance that read as most symmetric and proportioned
Reduces close-up lens distortion and shows preferred features
Face photographs more balanced and attractive
angle.text: Choosing a camera side, tilt and distance changes which features dominate the image. Practitioners step back from the lens, favour the side they find more symmetric and adjust height and tilt to emphasise the eyes and jawline in photos and video calls.
